name: Diego Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Diego, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at a zinc and lead mine, about nine hundred metres down. It's a low, long machine we call a bogger: it scoops the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass, which is a shaft that drops it to the crusher. I'm the shift lead for the loader crew on days, so I'm in the cage at half six, do the line-up with the boys and Karen, then I'm on the machine most of the shift. I like it when a stope is mucking out clean and the numbers on the board are good. What wears me out is the heat down there in summer and the drive home, which is forty minutes on a road with no lights.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has the way you work changed much in the time you've been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, slowly. When I started, you had a lamp and a radio and that was it. Now there's wifi underground, tags on our belts so they know where we are, and last year they brought in two tele-remote boggers you drive from a chair on the surface. I drove one from the surface for a shift last March, and the strangest thing was going home with clean hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, let's get back to talking about the things that actually matter, like ventilation and pay. At the tea break I'd say the chatbots can write the safety reports and leave the rest of us alone. Online I'd maybe share a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd say the tele-remote boggers are still coming whether AI is hype or not. They work, I've seen them. But they need a person in the chair, so a plateau means the job changes shape rather than disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and keep doing a shift or two in the remote chair when they offer it, so I'm not a stranger to it. I'd try to put fifty a week aside, because right now there's nothing. I'd vote for whoever's talking about protecting mine pensions, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, to be honest. It's the world I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's nothing saved right now. How did that happen for a senior man?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our company pays less than the big ones, maybe fifteen percent less, and there's nowhere else to go out here. Then my mother's funeral and the roof last year cleaned us out. Amira works at the aged care home, so we cover the bills, but there's no fat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter put one on my phone. I used it to write a complaint to the council about the road, and it was better than what I'd have written, I'll admit that. It wrote a better letter than me in ten seconds, and I've been writing to that council about the same pothole for six years.

S0.say: Let's get back to the things that matter, like ventilation and pay. The chatbots can write the safety reports and leave the rest of us alone.
S0.think: The tele-remote loaders are coming whether AI is hype or not, but they still need a person in the chair. A plateau means my job changes shape rather than disappears.
S0.do: Keeps working and takes remote-chair shifts when offered so the system isn't strange to him. Tries to save about fifty a week and votes for whoever promises to protect mine pensions.
S0.feel: Calm, because it is the world he already knows.
S0.quote: It wrote a better letter than me in ten seconds, and I've been writing to that council about the same pothole for six years.
S0.fieldNote: Diego has already driven a remote loader and is matter-of-fact about it. His thin savings come from lower company pay plus a funeral and a roof repair, not from carelessness. He uses AI occasionally and admitted, a little sheepishly, that it wrote a better letter than he could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine if workers share in it. If one person in a chair on the surface does the work of three boggers, then that person should be paid like it, and the other two should be retrained, not shown the gate. I'd say that at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think they'd keep one in three of us. The ones who can sit in the chair and watch four screens. I think I'd be one of the ones they keep, because I'm good and I've already done it, but the boys on my crew wouldn't all make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the full tele-remote course the first week it's offered, even if it means night training. I'd push the union to get the course open to everyone, not just the ones the managers like. And we'd cut the extras, the satellite TV and the takeaway on Fridays, and put that aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. I can see a path for me, but it's narrow, and I'd be walking it while my mates fall off the sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, who's fifty-two and can drive a bogger in his sleep but reads slowly. Karen, who's young and quick and would be fine. The ones who'll get picked aren't the best miners. They're the ones who are good on a computer, and that's not the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like for you, going from underground to a chair on the surface every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. I'd miss the crew in the lunch room, the joking. But my lungs would thank me, and Amira would sleep better. She's never said it, but I know she listens for the phone every shift.

S1.say: Change is fine if workers share in it: the person in the chair doing three loaders' work should be paid for it, and the others retrained, not shown the gate. He would say it at the union meeting.
S1.think: I think they'd keep about one in three of us, the ones who can sit in the chair and watch four screens. I'd probably be kept, but not all of my crew would make it.
S1.do: Signs up for the full tele-remote course in the first week, even if training is at night. Pushes the union to open the course to everyone and cuts satellite TV and Friday takeaway to save.
S1.feel: Anxious: there is a path for him, but it's narrow and his mates may fall off the sides.
S1.quote: The ones who'll get picked aren't the best miners. They're the ones who are good on a computer, and that's not the same thing.
S1.fieldNote: Diego is confident he could make the switch because he already has, and his worry is mostly for slower colleagues. His line about computer skill not being the same as mining skill was sharp. Moving to the surface also has an upside he hadn't voiced before: his partner's worry each shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when governments have to earn their pay. A wage guarantee, or a pension bridge for older miners, something. At the union I'd say we need to move this month, not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, in two years even the man in the chair goes. If the machine can drive itself and fix itself, they don't need me watching it. I'd be sixty, with a mortgage that has six years left on it and no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and the company to ask for a redundancy that pays out the mortgage, and I'd join any action to get it. I'd stop every spend that isn't food, power or fuel. I'd ask my son, who's an electrician in the city, whether there's work there for an old man who can fix hydraulics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, losing sleep. Like when the ground talks above you and you don't know which way to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years feel different from the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, retraining is pointless, because whatever I train for is gone too. With the slower ones, the tele-remote course buys me time. Two years doesn't give you time to learn a new job. It just gives you time to watch the old one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your son about work in the city. Would you really move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Amira's mother is in the home where she works, and she won't leave her. Maybe I'd go for weeks at a time and come back, like a fly-in, fly-out job in reverse. I'm not sure that's living, though.

S2.say: This is when governments have to earn their pay, with a wage guarantee or a pension bridge for older miners. The union needs to move this month, not next year.
S2.think: In two years even the man in the chair goes, because the machine drives and fixes itself. He would be sixty with six years left on the mortgage and no cushion.
S2.do: Asks the union and company for a redundancy big enough to pay off the mortgage and joins any action to win it. Cuts everything but food, power and fuel, and asks his son about hydraulics work in the city.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, like hearing the ground move overhead and not knowing which way to go.
S2.quote: Two years doesn't give you time to learn a new job. It just gives you time to watch the old one go.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture removes the remote-chair path that steadied Diego in the slower scenario. He sees retraining as pointless with so little time. Moving is tangled up with his partner's mother being in care, so he would rather commute for long stretches than relocate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's treat it like one. The union should negotiate the transition now, while the company still needs us to run the place. That's what I'd tell the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. I think I could stretch it: do the tele-remote course, be useful in the chair for three or four of those years, and leave just short of sixty-five. It's tight, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the tele-remote ticket and ask to move to the surface. I'd put the extra from not paying for my underground gear and boots into paying down the mortgage. I'd help the union put together a list of every older miner and their pension dates, so we can bargain for each of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan in my hands, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me get to the surface before the surface goes too. With five years I can ride the remote chair most of the way to the pension, like stepping across stones to the other bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home, if the mortgage has to come down faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camping trip we do every Easter at the lake, with the grandkids. That's the one that would hurt. Then the second car, Amira would have to get lifts to the home.

S3.say: Five years is a warning, so let's treat it like one. The union should negotiate the transition now, while the company still needs us to run the place.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, and I could ride the remote chair for three or four years and leave just short of sixty-five. It's tight, but it's a plan.
S3.do: Gets the tele-remote ticket in year one and moves to the surface, putting the savings into the mortgage. Helps the union list every older miner's pension date to bargain for each of them, and drops the Easter camping trip if needed.
S3.feel: Anxious, but having a plan helps a lot.
S3.quote: With five years I can ride the remote chair most of the way to the pension, like stepping across stones to the other bank.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Diego see a stepping-stone route to his pension through remote operation. His instinct is to organise for others too, listing every older miner's pension date. The Easter camping trip with the grandkids is the cut that would hurt most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it right, and if they don't, it's because they chose not to. I'd want the union pushing for a fund paid by the companies, to retrain the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm sixty-eight, so I'd be out before the end. My real worry is being pushed out early, at sixty-two or sixty-three, because the company starts thinning the older ones as it gets ready. That's how it usually goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as now in year one: keep working, take remote shifts, chip away at the mortgage. I'd write down a target date to retire and tell the company early, so they'd plan around me rather than over me. I'd join the union's training committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It's far enough away that I might just slip under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies thin out the older ones. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they mechanised the old shaft in 2009, they offered packages and the over-fifty-fives got leaned on to take them. Some went happy, some went angry. They don't sack you. They just keep asking how your knees are until you take the package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the young miners, with ten years to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them trained while they're still earning, not after they've been let go. And paid to learn, because none of them can afford to stop for six months, same as me.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it right, and if they don't, it's because they chose not to. The union should push for a company-funded fund to retrain the young ones.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight, so I'd be out before the end. My real worry is being pushed out early, at sixty-two or sixty-three, as the company thins out older workers.
S4.do: Keeps working, takes remote shifts and chips away at the mortgage in year one. Sets a retirement date and tells the company early, and joins the union's training committee.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not scared, because it's far enough away that he might slip under it.
S4.quote: They don't sack you. They just keep asking how your knees are until you take the package.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Diego expects to retire before AGI arrives, but he fears being eased out early. His memory of 2009, when older miners were leaned on to take packages, shaped that fear. He wants young miners paid to learn, linking their situation to his own thin savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, no time to learn anything, and a mortgage with six years left. What would help is a bridge to the pension for the older ones, and a mortgage break for families in mining towns while it settles. Paid retraining for the younger ones, not courses you have to pay for yourself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't money. Underground, you trust the man next to you with your life. I don't know who you trust when it's all machines and screens.

headlineQuote: I drove one from the surface for a shift last March, and the strangest thing was going home with clean hands.
portrait: Diego Farah is a 58-year-old shift lead on an underground loader crew at a zinc and lead mine, paid less than at the big companies and with nothing saved after a funeral and a roof repair. He is a union man who has already driven a remote loader from the surface and uses AI on his phone now and then. In the slower scenarios he sees remote operation as his path to the pension, though he worries for crewmates who are better miners than computer users. The two-year scenario takes that path away and leaves him alarmed, while ten years mostly makes him fear being eased out early.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to retrain and he still has six years left on the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to the pension for older miners, a mortgage break for families in mining towns, and paid retraining for younger workers.
